Closes #630

Some question
1. Is it fine for the `payload` as `null` when `stream` is sent?
2. Is `payload.on('end')` correct for `stream` handling and add trailers?
3. Is it fine for `trailer` only support sync function?

pr_comments:
> Is it fine for trailer only support sync function?

I feel like it's already supporting an asynchronous operation that by the time this callback is invoked all the inputs should be available to calculate the trailing values you need. 

At the same time, I can see it useful to support async callbacks for cases where someone might want to use an api call in order to calculate a value you want to send in a trailing header. I think this would make it most flexible, but would also give more rope to the framework user to do lots of extraneous network calls before resolving a header value. I suppose its not necessarily terrible since the response to the client has already been sent.

> I feel like it's already supporting an asynchronous operation that by the time this callback is invoked all the inputs should be available to calculate the trailing values you need.
> 
> At the same time, I can see it useful to support async callbacks for cases where someone might want to use an api call in order to calculate a value you want to send in a trailing header. I think this would make it most flexible, but would also give more rope to the framework user to do lots of extraneous network calls before resolving a header value. I suppose its not necessarily terrible since the response to the client has already been sent.

I can think of a solution for `async` trailer if the payload is `string` or `buffer`.
But when it comes to `stream`, it is a tough one as the `response` will end much sooner than I think.

At least, I need somebody help on the area of `stream` async trailer.

I'm not sure this is needed to solve the etag case. In the vast majority of cases we would want to return a 304 - the content can be cached. In that case you'd need to compute the etag before sending it. This is not very efficient.

As you can read at https://serverfault.com/questions/690341/algorithm-behind-nginx-etag-generation, NGINX does _not_ read the full file to compute the etag.

I have never found a good use case  for trailers and in practices they are not very commonly used.

> I'm not sure this is needed to solve the etag case. In the vast majority of cases we would want to return a 304 - the content can be cached. In that case you'd need to compute the etag before sending it. This is not very efficient.
> 
> As you can read at https://serverfault.com/questions/690341/algorithm-behind-nginx-etag-generation, NGINX does _not_ read the full file to compute the etag.
> 
> I have never found a good use case for trailers and in practices they are not very commonly used.

I never use the `trailers` before, but if somebody need it. The current code do not support it in a good way.
It must compute the trailers before sending the content, that means the trailers isn't take advantage of trailers anymore.

I am good with the current proposal for the minimal support of `trailers`. 
It can return the `Server-Timing` like the discussed issue.

That's cool!
I feel like `Server-Timing` might be worth to be a plugin on its own. But exposing core metrics of Fastify might be a good thing to be consumed by the `Server-timing` plugin. Don't you think so?
I'd see some kind of api like:

```js
fastify.get('/', function (request, reply) {
  reply.addTiming('reqLifecycle', rrequest.RequestLifecyleTime)
  reply.addTiming('routingTime', request.RoutingTime)
  reply.send(data)
})
```

Edit: ok there already is a Server-Timing plugin my bad

> I'm not sure this is needed to solve the etag case. In the vast majority of cases we would want to return a 304 - the content can be cached. In that case you'd need to compute the etag before sending it. This is not very efficient.
> 
> As you can read at https://serverfault.com/questions/690341/algorithm-behind-nginx-etag-generation, NGINX does _not_ read the full file to compute the etag.
> 
> I have never found a good use case for trailers and in practices they are not very commonly used.

This is from MDN:
```
The method by which ETag values are generated is not specified. Typically, the ETag value is a hash of the content, a hash of the last modification timestamp, or just a revision number. 
```
There are two types of etags, weak and strong. Date and content length hashes are a good approach at generated weak etags. But if some content has a one character typo that is correct then, for example, a base64 hash of date+contentLength would not be great.

In regards to having to read the full file contents up front, that scenario is only necessary if the client has sent a `If-Match` or an `If-None-Match` header, in which case you'd need to read the file contents and calculate the strong etag to check for the match. Otherwise, if no headers then the client can receive the contents asap and the etag in a trailer.

> In regards to having to read the full file contents up front, that scenario is only necessary if the client has sent a If-Match or an If-None-Match header, in which case you'd need to read the file contents and calculate the strong etag to check for the match. Otherwise, if no headers then the client can receive the contents asap and the etag in a trailer.

Considering how CDNs works, the `if-match` and `if-none-match` cases are the most common ones. You shouldn't be serving files from Node.js anyway.

> > In regards to having to read the full file contents up front, that scenario is only necessary if the client has sent a If-Match or an If-None-Match header, in which case you'd need to read the file contents and calculate the strong etag to check for the match. Otherwise, if no headers then the client can receive the contents asap and the etag in a trailer.
> 
> Considering how CDNs works, the `if-match` and `if-none-match` cases are the most common ones. You shouldn't be serving files from Node.js anyway.

I'm not sure what you mean here, I shouldn't be serving files from node.js? This is confusing, isn't that what fastify.js is basically facilitating here? And yes, if-match/if-none-match are the most common cases, how do you suppose the CDN validates the etags it has cached with the etags its receiving from clients like browsers if not to ask an origin server that may or may not be running fastify.js? I'm confused as to what you're implying.

> I'm not sure what you mean here, I shouldn't be serving files from node.js?

NGINX and others provide better performance for serving files from disk.

> And yes, if-match/if-none-match are the most common cases, how do you suppose the CDN validates the etags it has cached with the etags its receiving from clients like browsers if not to ask an origin server that may or may not be running fastify.js?

Browser (not cached) -> CDN (cached) -> `If-None-Match` header is automatically added by the CDN -> Fastify.

Therefore you are almost always hitting the case of having to compute the etag before starting to send the content. Doing it as a trailer only adds complexity with extremely limited gain.

Finally quite a few CDNs do not support trailers.

I'm trying for that gain as this does not apply to a simple single website. Our cluster runs lots of websites and we incur millions of requests per half hour, so small incremental gains all add up quickly, which is why I was trying to do it with this approach, and our CDN supports them just fine.

We also use fastify.js because our entire application and build pipeline is entirely javascript, and our web server doesn't only serve static files, that is just a portion of the application.

issue_context.title: Support HTTP/1.1 trailers
issue_context.body: as titled, I think `reply` might needs some facility to set trailers. It might also be a bad idea, as the actual response is always accessible and they could be set in that way if we want to.
comments: @mcollina How common is it to use `trailing headers` ? Is it worth to pull it up to fastify? After some research, I found out that even Hapi, Koa2 has no support for this. I'm not against this.
I don’t think they are common, so maybe we can avoid them altogether. But it’s a discussion that’s worth having.
I can confidently say that I have never used them. And I can _almost_ as confidently say I have never seen them used.
@fastify/fastify anyone else have an opinion?
I've never used them, never seen them used, and I'm not sure if I'll ever need to use them.
Closing for now, but we can revisit anytime!

It would be nice to offer semantic support for trailers. The handler has to specify the trailer keys in headers, then stream the response, then set the trailer header. Maybe something like this:

```js
reply.trailer("etag", async (reply, next) => { return calculatedEtagValue });
```

After the body stream is complete, the trailer callbacks would be executed and they would return their value to be stored in Node's http.response.addTrailers().

This may be better served as a plugin.
I have a feeling this might only be served by implementing it in the framework. Anyway, would you like to work on this?

Maybe so. I can imagine the `Server-Timing` plugin would be interested in using it.

I'll hack at a plugin first to see how much effort it is.

etags are the exact reason I ended up on this thread. I'm trying to send a file stream in reply.send() and I'm piping the stream to a hash so I can calculate an etag value that I want to send as a trailing header. @mattbishop did  you ever make any headway on this?

I think it is not hard to make it success using `onSend` hook.

Generally speaking,
1. If you pass `object`, `string` in `payload`. It will be `string` in `onSend` hook and we can embed the `trailers` easily.
2. If you pass `buffer` in `payload`. It will be `buffer` in `OnSend`, it should be almost the same case as `1.`.
3. If you pass `stream` in `payload`. It will be `stream` in `OnSend` and we need to create a new `stream` for piping the original  stream and add the `trailers` at the end.
Seems interesting, if ok I’ll give it a try during the weekend. I see this mostly in a form of a plugin. I’ll shake my head around it

Sorry, I spoke too soon. I left the old code in place and so the console output was wrong, you can see the output is actually missing the `>` character I have in the example code, my mistake. 

After I fixed that, the RTE went away, but the headers aren't sent.

```shell
> etag is: 3880014421
sent etag
```

But the headers aren't there:
```
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK

< edge-cache-tag: develop
< cache-tag: develop
< xkey: develop
< Date: Thu, 24 Mar 2022 22:46:33 GMT

```
It's missing the `etag` header I'm trying to set.

> @climba03003 If I turn the onSend hook to an async function and then await on the calculation of the header value before I return the payload, doesn't that effectively block the response until the header is computed? Cause if so I could simply just calculate the header before even sending the response and add it via normal means.
> 
> But I'm trying to do it without blocking the response which is why I was trying to pipe the response stream into another stream object that hashes the contents. Then I was attaching a finish event handler to read the hash and add the value as a trailing header:
> 
> ```js
> const onSendHook = async (request, reply, payload) => {
>   if (!reply.getHeader('etag') && typeof payload.pipe === 'function') {
>     const hasher = new Stream(0xCACACAFE)
>     const stream = payload.pipe(hasher)
>     stream.on('finish', () => {
>       const etag = hasher.read()
>       console.log(`> etag is: ${etag}`)
>       reply.raw.addTrailers({ etag })
>       console.log('sent etag')
>     })
>   }
> }
> ```

Since, we are using `response.end(payload)` or `payload.pipe(response)` in the code.
You cannot send any `trailer` afterward. That's why it am awaiting the `trailers` before sending any.

https://github.com/fastify/fastify/blob/802e3e8935dd8a84e08330faca83b7f7a108dad2/lib/reply.js#L394-L433

If the order need to be correct, it needs to update the core for this feature.

Yea it makes sense now. I was trying to do it in this order basically to try to incur as little cost to the response time by not awaiting a header value but still be able to calculate a deterministic etag header based on the file contents.

short question: how would you generate an etag trailer for a stream using the "native" supported trailers now?
This might become more relevant in the ecosystem, since react now supports streaming.

However, I'm not sure if it even makes sense, since the stream is getting streamed to the client before the etag can be generated, so everything is already at the client when the client finds out the etag matches - so with streams there can't be any 304 responses? Did I miss anything?

> However, I'm not sure if it even makes sense, since the stream is getting streamed to the client before the etag can be generated, so everything is already at the client when the client finds out the etag matches - so with streams there can't be any 304 responses? Did I miss anything?

No this is a good analysis. Streaming with React SSR can only be cached with a TTL, no etags.

As I said elsewhere, trailers are of limited utility.
